stem: Your application's traffic spikes during the day and drops at night. You want to add capacity when demand rises and remove it when demand falls, paying only for what you use. Which cloud benefit best describes this?

options.text: A large upfront capital investment in fixed hardware
Fixed on-premises capacity sized for peak

explanationCorrect: Elasticity is the ability to acquire resources as demand rises and release them as it falls, so you match capacity to load and pay only for what you use.
explanationIncorrect: A large upfront capital investment in fixed hardware is the traditional on-premises model the cloud moves away from; it is capital expenditure that does not shrink when demand drops. Vendor lock-in is a risk to weigh, not a benefit, and it is unrelated to scaling with demand. Provisioning fixed on-premises capacity sized for peak means you pay for the peak all the time and still cannot easily scale beyond it. The property of growing and shrinking with demand and paying for use is elasticity.

stem: Moving from buying and owning servers up front to paying only for the compute you actually consume represents which cloud value proposition?

options.text: Trading capital expense (CapEx) for variable operating expense (OpEx)
Increasing CapEx while removing all OpEx

explanationCorrect: The cloud lets you replace large up-front hardware purchases (CapEx) with pay-as-you-go spending (OpEx), so you pay for consumption instead of owning depreciating assets.
explanationIncorrect: The model reduces CapEx, it does not increase it. It does not eliminate costs; you still pay for what you use. Fixed multi-year hardware leases are the opposite of variable, consumption-based spending. The value proposition is trading CapEx for OpEx.

stem: What is the relationship between an AWS Region and an Availability Zone?

options.text: A Region is a geographic area that contains multiple, physically separate Availability Zones
An Availability Zone contains many Regions
A Region and an Availability Zone are the same thing
A Region is a single building and an Availability Zone is a single server

explanationCorrect: A Region is a geographic area, and within it are multiple Availability Zones, each one or more physically separate data centers, which is what enables highly available designs.
explanationIncorrect: The containment is the other way around: Regions contain Availability Zones, not the reverse. They are not the same thing; a Region groups several AZs. An AZ is more than a single server and a Region more than a single building; each AZ is one or more data centers. A Region contains multiple AZs.

stem: To keep an application available even if one data center fails, how should you deploy it across AWS?

options.text: Across multiple Availability Zones within a Region
On a single large instance in one Availability Zone
On one Availability Zone with a larger disk

explanationCorrect: Spreading across multiple Availability Zones means a failure confined to one AZ does not take the whole application down, which is the standard high-availability pattern.
explanationIncorrect: A single instance in one AZ is a single point of failure; if that AZ fails, so does the app. An edge location caches content for delivery; it is not where you run a resilient application tier. A bigger disk in one AZ adds capacity but no fault isolation. High availability comes from multiple Availability Zones.

stem: Adding more instances to handle increased load, rather than making one instance bigger, is called what?
explanationCorrect: Adding more instances to share the load is horizontal scaling, or scaling out, which improves both capacity and fault tolerance.
explanationIncorrect: Vertical scaling means resizing a single instance to a larger type, which is the opposite of adding more instances. Diagonal scaling is not a standard term. Manual failover is switching to a standby after a failure, not a scaling strategy. Adding instances is horizontal scaling.

stem: Which of the following is one of the pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
explanationCorrect: Operational Excellence is one of the Well-Architected pillars, alongside Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
explanationIncorrect: Maximum vendor lock-in, manual provisioning, and single point of failure are anti-patterns, not framework pillars; the framework exists to help you avoid exactly those. The genuine pillar listed is Operational Excellence.

stem: An organization runs some workloads in its own on-premises data center and others in AWS, integrated together. Which deployment model is this?
explanationCorrect: Combining on-premises infrastructure with cloud resources that work together is the hybrid cloud deployment model.
explanationIncorrect: Pure public cloud would run everything in AWS with no on-premises component. Pure private cloud would keep everything in the organization's own data center. Multi-tenant SaaS describes a software delivery model, not a mix of on-premises and cloud infrastructure. Mixing on-premises and cloud is hybrid.

stem: A startup wants to serve users in Europe and Asia quickly without building its own data centers on those continents. Which cloud benefit enables this?

options.text: Going global in minutes by deploying into AWS Regions around the world
Buying land and constructing new data centers abroad
Shipping physical servers overseas by freight
Restricting the application to a single Region

explanationCorrect: AWS's global footprint lets you deploy into Regions near your users in minutes, so you reach new geographies without owning infrastructure there.
explanationIncorrect: Constructing data centers and shipping servers are exactly the slow, capital-heavy steps the cloud removes. Restricting to one Region would increase latency for distant users, the opposite of the goal. The benefit is going global in minutes across AWS Regions.

stem: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system running on an Amazon EC2 instance?

options.text: No one, because EC2 guest operating systems never need patching

explanationCorrect: In the shared responsibility model AWS secures the infrastructure (security of the cloud) while the customer is responsible for what they run on it (security in the cloud), which for EC2 includes patching the guest operating system.
explanationIncorrect: AWS is responsible for the physical facilities, hardware, and the virtualization layer, not the operating system you install and manage on an instance. A Marketplace vendor supplies an image but does not manage patching on your running instances over time. And guest operating systems certainly do require patching, so leaving it to no one is not an option. For EC2, patching the guest OS is squarely the customer's responsibility.

stem: You need durable, virtually unlimited object storage for backups and static website assets, and you want to be billed for the amount of data you store. Which AWS service fits?
explanationCorrect: Amazon S3 is object storage designed for high durability and effectively unlimited capacity, billed largely on how much you store, which matches backups and static assets exactly.
explanationIncorrect: Amazon EC2 provides virtual compute instances; it runs your code but is not an object store, and you pay for compute rather than stored objects. Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service for structured, queryable data, not a bucket for files and backups. AWS IAM manages identities and permissions and stores no application data at all. The durable, virtually unlimited object storage service is Amazon S3.

stem: You have a steady, predictable EC2 workload that will run continuously for the next year and you want the lowest price in exchange for a commitment. Which purchasing option is most cost-effective?

options.text: A one-year Reserved Instance or Compute Savings Plan commitment
Spot Instances for the always-on production workload
Dedicated Hosts billed hourly with no commitment

explanationCorrect: For steady, predictable usage over a term, a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan gives a substantial discount over On-Demand in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment, which is the cheapest fit for a known long-running workload.
explanationIncorrect: On-Demand has no commitment and the highest per-hour rate, so it is the wrong choice when usage is predictable and you could commit for a discount. Spot Instances are cheapest per hour but can be reclaimed with little notice, which makes them unsuitable for an always-on production workload that must not be interrupted. Dedicated Hosts address licensing and isolation needs and cost more, not less, so they do not minimize price for a normal workload. The cost-effective choice for predictable long-running usage is a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan commitment.

stem: You want to reduce latency for users around the world by serving your application's static content from locations physically close to them. Which AWS service provides this content delivery network?
explanationCorrect: Amazon CloudFront is AWS's content delivery network: it caches content at edge locations worldwide and serves each user from a nearby edge, cutting latency.
explanationIncorrect: Amazon VPC is a private virtual network for isolating and connecting your AWS resources; it does not distribute content to global edge locations. AWS CloudTrail records API activity for auditing and governance and has nothing to do with content delivery. Amazon SQS is a message queue for decoupling application components, not a CDN. The global content delivery network is Amazon CloudFront.
